articles.title: Last Week on My Mac: Storage crisis management
articles.subtitle: You're running out of free space, so check in Storage settings to see where it has all gone. System Data has reached 50 GB, but what is that, and what should you do to reduce it?
articles.author: The Eclectic Light Company
articles.content:
There’s a great more to storage management than freeing up space as outlined by Apple. Although the Storage section in System Settings is becoming increasingly useful, neither that nor the support note even mentions snapshots, and their coverage of caches is vague at best. Search Google instead and you’ll be offered expensive subscriptions to housekeeping apps or, if you’re really unlucky, a link to a ClickFix attack.

Storage management has been built into Mac operating systems since classic times, and when QuickLook was introduced in Mac OS X 10.5 Leopard 19 years ago, one of its essential features was maintaining its thumbnail cache. Yet some recent comments about purging caches blame them on APFS, a relative newcomer, but that is at least responsible for the addition of snapshots to storage management.

macOS and its constituent processes are prolific cachers, and have been for many years. Those caches are a double-edged sword, accelerating many features in the human interface and beyond, at a modest cost of a little disk space. Without both caching to disk and caching in memory, features like the Finder’s Gallery view would be unusable, as would much of QuickLook itself.

Custom thumbnails were introduced in Classic Mac OS around 1988-91, when they were generated for images by the apps that edited them, then saved to an ICN# resource in that file’s Resource fork, which was effectively a cached thumbnail. To render a view containing multiple thumbnails, the Finder then had to look in each file’s Resource fork and convert its ICN# resource for display. Other types of document were out of luck, though, as apps didn’t save their thumbnails as they did with images.

QuickLook took on the task of converting the contents of a wide range of different file types to thumbnail images, using qlgenerator plug-ins, and saving those in its cache. When the Finder wanted multiple thumbnails to display in a view, instead of looking in each file individually, all it had to was to find their cached thumbnails, a task performed by iconservicesd.

That’s fast enough for a responsive interface until it comes to scrolling through larger thumbnails in a Gallery view. For that, not only do all those thumbnails need to be cached to disk, but as many as possible need to be cached in memory as well.

The most accessible caches are those used by web browsers like Safari. The benefits they bring can be shown most readily too, by simply emptying their caches repeatedly when trying to access some familiar websites. The command to Empty Caches is available in Safari’s Develop menu, added by enabling Show features for web developers in its Advanced settings. You’ll soon appreciate the value added by its caching.

Snapshots are one of the neater features in APFS, particularly for those whose laptops can’t always be within range of their backup storage. However, because they include almost every file in a volume, it’s all too common for them to capture huge and ever-changing data such as virtual machines. With a little careful planning, those can be stored in volumes that aren’t included in snapshots, and backed up separately when they’re inactive and offline.

Our increasingly jaundiced view of storage management in macOS hasn’t been helped by the opaque System Data category in Storage settings, when it’s able to complete calculating successfully. Its remit is so broad that it might be better named Anything and Everything Else.

I think I’ve got a reasonably good idea of what’s meant by purgeable space in Disk Utility, but I still haven’t a clue to the scope of what System Data includes, other than Apple’s unforthcoming definition as “the storage space used by all Apple and third-party files that don’t belong to any more specific category. ”

When free space is running low and you turn to Storage settings to see where it has gone, 50 GB of System Data is sufficient to put even an advanced user into a panic. Would deleting some snapshots help? Do some caches need to be deleted, and if so, which and how? Look for those answers in Apple’s documentation and you’ll be disappointed.

But the underlying problem is that storage management shouldn’t be about such crises, just as financial management isn’t about what to do when you’re overspent. There’s just so little reliable and detailed information about storage management, particularly from Apple.

articles.title: Onimusha: Way of the Sword proves the parry formula is far from stale, you just need to get freaky with it
articles.subtitle: Parry fatigue? Not me.
articles.author: PC Gamer
articles.content:
Listen, I'll be the first to admit that I'm a little biased towards parry-based action games. Sekiro will forever be my favourite FromSoftware game because of just how excellently it captured the back-and-forth feeling of swordplay, not only with its timed deflection mechanic, but its mandate to have you keep the pressure on.

But I appreciate that, for some, parry fatigue might be setting in. My fellow writer Mollie Taylor's sick of it, for instance—and I do understand. I think there are some games which use it as a bit of a crutch, and even the ones that don't can wear out their welcome.

Take Clair Obscur: Expedition 33, for instance. I liked it, but I wouldn't want every turn-based RPG I play to have a timed block in it. Still, it's fun to have the occasional one where stats can be overcome with deft enough bumper hands.

But to paint every parry-based system with the same brush seems short-sighted to me, because this deceptively simple mechanic has a ton of juice still left inside it: no other game proves this more than Onimusha: Way of the Sword, which, as far as I'm concerned, has broken new ground in terms of what parries can do.

Onimusha has one parry button, or at least, it has one parry button on the surface: your block, which when timed just as a blow is coming in, will send a series of sparks flying. The trick that Onimusha pulls—and most good parry-based games will do this—is in actually giving you several parry buttons. Onimusha is parries all the way down. You've got:

The parry. Hit the block button at the right time and see sparks fly.

Your deflect, an advanced version of the basic parry that requires you to hit another button while blocking.

The Issin counter, a parry for people with huge cajones with massive risk and massive reward.

This is the trick to making a parry-based action system feel good, like finely-chopping veggies so you don't notice them in your soup. Not only do each of these parry-like mechanics have a unique attack they counter, they also serve different purposes, giving you a toolbox of ripostes to your enemy's assault.

The basic parry builds up a meter, the Blazing State, which increases your damage and stagger—naturally graduating you to the more demanding deflect ability as time goes on once it's full. Deflecting also counters unavoidable attacks.

The genius here is in the back-and-forth minigame between parrying and deflecting, since your Blazing State depletes over time, and refreshing it is easier than building it up from scratch. Meaning that even when your sword's on fire and you're deflecting, you still want to throw in the odd parry to keep your weapon ignited.

Then there's the Issin counter, my beloved. The extremely tight window for using this thing seems too punishing at first, but Onimusha throws in highly-telegraphed attacks for you as a treat—these are Issin bait. Slow, ponderous swings with clean windows that'll have you salivating the moment you see their wind-up.

It's often said that Sekiro: Shadows Die Twice is a rhythm game in disguise, and the same is true with Onimusha. And just like DDR has multiple directional arrows to keep things interesting, so too do these games grant you a broad toolkit, one that both locks you into an engaging and fatal game of rock, paper scissors.

There's also that sliding scale of risk, too, the progression from parrying, to deflecting to Issin counters encourages you to make more daring plays. The easiest defensive option gives the smallest reward, whereas an Issin counter shears off a huge chunk of health and stamina from your foe. And even then, both Issin and the deflect are riskier for different reasons!

Deflecting has a more complicated set of button presses, like trying to throw out a dragon punch in a fighting game, whereas Issin has strict timing requirements.

Onimusha's at the forefront of parry experimentation, but it's not the only one. My favourite non-standard parry, outside of Onimusha, is in Nine Sols' Unbounded Counter. You hold a different block button, are vulnerable for a short-wind up, and then are given a short window whereupon releasing the button creates a parry.

Hold it for too long, and you'll whiff, opening yourself up with another window of vulnerability. It requires you to know an attack's coming three business days in advance, which is why it feels so good to pull off.

Point being, I think the parry gets a bad reputation because it's viewed as an overly simple solution to engaging action combat—fie, I say! I bite my thumb at thee! Parries, like any other game mechanic, can be ham-fisted in their implementation. But they can also be very, very clever.

articles.title: Claude chats exposed in Google searches – another endorsement of Apple’s privacy approach
articles.subtitle: We’ve long cautioned against disclosing sensitive personal data in AI chatbot sessions, given that most companies use these as training data, but there’s now an even bigger reason.
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apple Intelligence
articles.content:
We’ve long cautioned against disclosing sensitive personal data in AI chatbot sessions, given that most companies use these as training data, but there’s now an even bigger reason.

Things got way worse over the weekend when Redditors discovered that you could access some Claude AI chats through a simple Google search …

Claude chats exposed

Claude has a share option that allows you to share a chat session with a colleague, friend or family member. The chatbot generates a link you can send to one or more individuals, and Claude implictly assures you that nobody can see the chat knowing the URL.

To share a chat: Click the “Share” button in the upper right corner of your chat. Once a chat has been shared, anyone with the link can view the chat snapshot.

The problem is that Redditors discovered you don’t in fact need the link to be able to view the chat. You can simply Google for it, either using specific search terms or just asking Google to show you all of the chats that have been shared in this way. BBC News reports:

Hundreds of user conversations with Anthropic’s popular artificial intelligence (AI) chatbot Claude were found to have been available to essentially anyone online […] Users on Reddit initially discovered, external the publicly available chats, which covered more than 200 conversations with Claude across at least 25 pages of search results – some taking place just weeks ago.

Literally all you had to do was tell google to search the directory used for shared Claude chats (site:claude.ai/share).

As you might expect, some of the chat sessions were completely unhinged, like asking why the record industry was hiding the fact that birds co-wrote most of Jay-Z’s albums. But others contained extremely sensitive information, such as transcripts of private conversations; a lawyer asking if they needed to self-report a breach of conduct; and a user asking for help creating a crypto wallet, and exposing their keys in the process.

Anthropic has so far attempted to claim that this is not a problem.

When someone shares a conversation, they are making that content publicly accessible, and like other public web content, it may be archived by third-party services.

The reality, of course, is that it is very much a problem, since this is not at all what users would expect. Worse, a Wired reports suggests that the underlying cause appears to be gross incompetence.

WIRED reviewed a sample of the exposed Claude chat pages and found that they did not include the “noindex” tag that both Bing and Google say they take into consideration when deciding whether or not to index a page […] Anthropic didn’t respond to questions about why it didn’t include the “noindex” tag on the shared chat pages.

It follows yesterday’s news about Claude Cowork being able to escape its sandbox on Mac and gain full access to all files.

How to protect yourself

The problem appears to have been at least partially addressed for now, with previously available search results now failing, but I would advise against using the share feature given that it relies on security by obscurity.

I’d also advise removing any past shared chats. You can do this in Settings > Privacy > Shared chats > Manage.

Another endorsement of Apple’s approach

articles.title: Persona 4 Revival Finds Its Kanji, And It Isn't Troy Baker Or Matt Mercer
articles.subtitle: Daman Mills is the new voice actor of Kanji Tatsumi in Persona 4 Revival During the past PAX West panel for Persona 4 Revival, Atlus showed off the sizzle reel trailer for Kanji Tatsumi, one of the game's most-discussed characters.
articles.author: Polygon
articles.content:
Daman Mills is the new voice actor of Kanji Tatsumi in Persona 4 Revival

During the past PAX West panel for Persona 4 Revival, Atlus showed off the sizzle reel trailer for Kanji Tatsumi, one of the game's most-discussed characters. While this role has previously been portrayed by Troy Baker and Matt Mercer, Atlus' latest Persona remake will feature a brand-new voice actor for Kanji.

Who is the new voice actor for Kanji Tatsumi?

Daman Mills has been confirmed as the new voice actor for Kanji Tatsumi. Mills is best known for being the current voice of Frieza in the Dragon Ball franchise, but has also portrayed characters in games like Borderlands 3, Final Fantasy VII Remake, and Yakuza Kiwami 3.

He has worked with Atlus quite a bit in the past too, voicing Aogami in Shin Megami Tensei 5, Madam Ginko in Soul Hackers 2, Takaya Sakaki in Persona 3 Reload, and Auch in Unicorn Overlord. Considering Atlus is recasting everyone for this remake, it's not too surprising they called upon Daman Mills to voice this Persona 4 character.

Kanji Tatsumi is an important character for this remake to get right. Not only has he been voiced by Troy Baker and Matt Mercer, two of the industry's most iconic voice actors, but he's also an early example of a prominent video game character really exploring their gender identity in-game. While there's some controversy surrounding how other characters like Yosuke treat Kanji in Persona 4, this remake will address that.

"While he has a more masculine-leaning approach with, like, his whole identity, he also has some femininity to him as well that I really like and admire," Mills said of Kanji during the panel. "Though, I think for Kanji, it leads to some insecurities overall within the story, and for him, it makes him a little bit afraid because it's not necessarily a social norm.

But we gradually see him sort of progress through that within the story and sort of face those trials and growth, and it has just been such an incredible thing to experience, and I really enjoy the character very much. "

Persona 4 Revival will be released for PS5, Windows PC, and Xbox Series X on Feb. 18, 2027. It'll be available on Game Pass from day one.

articles.title: iPhone 18 Pro: Everything M6 Tells Us About the A20 Chip
articles.subtitle: Apple announced the M6 chip last week, just ahead of its September iPhone event, providing the clearest indication yet of what the A20 will bring to the iPhone 18 lineup.
articles.author: MacRumors
articles.content:
Apple announced the M6 chip last week, just ahead of its September iPhone event, providing the clearest indication yet of what the A20 will bring to the iPhone 18 lineup.

Apple silicon generations share much of their architecture across the A-series and the M-series, so a new A-series chip normally functions as a partial preview of the M-series chip that follows it. This year the order reversed; the M6 was revealed on August 25, ahead of the A20 Pro expected in the iPhone 18 Pro this month.

Recent reports place the A20 Pro at up to 18% faster and up to 30% more power efficient than the A19 Pro, which is broadly similar to the M6 over the M5.

Apple's First 2nm iPhone Chip

The M6 is Apple's first chip built on TSMC's 2nm (N2) process, with the second almost certain to be the A20. Being a smaller manufacturing process, N2 has higher transistor density, allowing Apple to pack more performance into a smaller area.

Apple has historically debuted new nodes on the A-series, since iPhone volume validates yields, so introducing N2 in an $899 Mac mini represents a change. As such, reports that the A20 and A20 Pro will move to N2 are now supported by a shipping product rather than analyst predictions. The consequence for the iPhone event is that the "Apple's first 2nm chip" claim is no longer available.

Dual Neural Engine?

The iPhone's Neural Engine has remained at 16 cores and approximately 35 trillion operations per second since the A17 Pro, spanning three generations. The M6 introduces a Dual 16-core Neural Engine, which Apple says system frameworks can address simultaneously for up to 2x the peak compute of previous generations.

The change corresponds with the reported move to WMCM packaging, which integrates memory onto the same wafer as the CPU, GPU, and Neural Engine to shorten the path between them. It is possible that die area and thermal constraints may limit a dual engine to the A20 Pro.

GPU AI Gains Are Now Incremental

Apple said the M5 delivered over 4x the peak GPU compute for AI compared to the M4, reflecting the introduction of Neural Accelerators within each GPU core. The M6 is rated at nearly 30% over the M5.

The A19 Pro recorded a comparable 4x improvement on the iPhone 17 Pro last September for the same architectural reason. Second-generation Neural Accelerators consequently appear to represent a refinement rather than another step change, suggesting the A20 Pro will not repeat the A19 Pro's headline figure.

Graphics Improvements Should Carry Across

The M6 adds 50% increased geometry rates, an updated shader core architecture, revised Dynamic Caching, and hardware-accelerated ray tracing. These are architectural changes and comparable graphics work has historically appeared across both the A-series and M-series within the same generation.

Memory Bandwidth Suggests a Modest A20 Gain

Memory bandwidth determines how quickly data moves between the memory and the processor, and it is the main constraint on running large language models on device. The M6 provides up to 170GB/s, which Apple describes as a 10% increase over the M5's 153.6GB/s.

That increase is small enough to indicate Apple is using a faster grade of the same LPDDR5X memory rather than moving to the newer LPDDR6 standard, which would have delivered a far larger jump. Reports indicate Apple is sourcing high-speed LPDDR5X from Samsung for the ‌iPhone 18‌ lineup, and the M6 is consistent with that.

The implication for the A20 is that memory bandwidth is unlikely to improve dramatically. The A19 Pro is rated at 76.8GB/s, and a similar 10% uplift would take the A20 Pro to roughly 85GB/s. Any meaningful gain in how quickly the ‌iPhone 18 Pro‌ loads and runs on-device models is therefore more likely to come from WMCM packaging shortening the distance data travels than from the memory itself.

Meta is launching Muse Voice Transcribe, its first real-time audio perception model. It brings multilingual, streaming transcription to Meta AI for Mac, Muse Code, and developers through the Meta Model API.

Muse Voice Transcribe powers system-wide dictation on Mac

Meta Superintelligence Labs says Muse Voice Transcribe combines streaming automatic speech recognition with speaker diarization and endpointing.

In practical terms, it can transcribe speech as it happens, separate speakers across recordings with 20-plus voices, and determine when someone has finished talking, all without a separate post-processing step.

The model was trained across more than 70 languages, with 25 validated at launch. It supports audio longer than an hour, plus native code-switching within or between sentences. Language, keyword, and context biasing can further improve recognition.

Rather than using one fixed tradeoff between speed and accuracy, Muse Voice Transcribe decides how long to listen before committing each word. Meta calls this “adaptive delay.” The system can move quickly through easier speech while using more audio context for difficult words.

Meta says the model ranks first on the Artificial Analysis streaming speech-to-text leaderboard as of September 1.

Muse Voice Transcribe is available today through the Meta Model API for $3 per 1,000 audio-minutes, equivalent to $0.18 per hour.

It is also already powering dictation in Meta AI for Mac and Muse Code. On Mac, users can hold the Fn key to dictate into any application.

articles.title: I never thought a fishing sim could be this fun, but How to Fish proves me wrong with its ridiculous physics, killer spider crabs, and classic co-op chaos
articles.subtitle: I now know How to Fish, kinda.
articles.author: PC Gamer
articles.content:
I stand knee deep in a pool of blood. My coworkers, comrades, and friends reduced to food for soulless seagulls. Give a man a fish and he may throw it into the mouth of a weary fisherman, teach a man to fish and he shall bring forth the wrath of a spider crab who knows how to stab you with your own knife.

This was my first experience of the new multiplayer fishing sim How to Fish, and now I can see why it's become such a smash-hit among bored and borderline-violent friendship groups.

It has a simple premise: you and up to four friends learn how to fish. The cycle of work involves players buying a basic fishing rod at first, using this to fish for, well, fish and crustaceans, and then beating them to death with your bare knuckles, brass knuckles, or a sick-ass knife.

Then you can either eat your catch to replenish your health or hunger or feed it to the lonely fisherman who sits on the dock and gives you coins for your hard work. With the coins gained you can buy more tools to help you fish, like the knife, or supplies which you can use as bait, such as half a hotdog or an empty beer can.

When I first woke up on the island I was met with a friendly punch in the face.

Some things can be so simple that they become boring, and perhaps How to Fish would fall into this trap, if it were just you and the fisherman on the island. But when you add three other people with nothing to lose and access to friendly-fire things get out of hand in the best way possible.

When I first woke up on the island I was met with a friendly punch in the face. From there on out my friends and I worked together, with the occasional fist fight, to get our cash stash up and resources ready to defeat our first boss. Oh, remember when I mentioned health? Yeah, this is why you need it.

It turns out that using a beer can to fish will lure in a monstrous spider crab who emerges from the ocean with the rage that only the pinnacle of evolution could muster. The music changes and a massive health bar appears—you must defeat this beast to continue to learn how to fish.

Our first encounter happened almost by accident and we were not prepared for it. We were cut down in no time at all and I was even carried off by a hungry seagull. The second fight went a little better, however.

I decided to take a back foot, as I was the only person armed with brass knuckles and not a knife. Instead of fighting I acted as medic, slapping my deceased comrades back to life while screaming "You don't get to give up on me yet!" Their poor dazed bodies would then stumble back into the fight against the spider crab, powered by my inspirational words and some clams.

I did get a couple of punches in while the crab was dazed. We even managed to get its health bar down past the final third. But alas, we failed and my body was once again flown off into the sunset by a hungry seagull.

We unfortunately had to cut our session short, but that hasn't stopped us from planning our next hunt. I certainly can't wait to get stuck back in to beat some fish and maybe learn how to actually fish. I've also got my eye on that sniper rifle and other guns which you can buy later on—that'll show that damn spider crab.

Dark Cherry was another major trend, with Baseus, ESR and Momax betting on the rumored iPhone 18 Pro color becoming 2026’s must-have shade. articles.title: Blending Deus Ex with Escape from Butcher Bay, Deficit is one of the best-feeling indie immersive sims I've played—even if the stealth system needs serious work
articles.subtitle: Playing the demo for Deficit was far from a net loss.
articles.author: PC Gamer
articles.content:
Immersive sims like Deus Ex and Dishonored are among the hardest kinds of games to make, so I always try to be supportive when an indie developer takes on the absurd challenge of creating one. Yet while there have been some good examples in recent years like Skin Deep and New Blood's early access Thief-like Gloomwood, a lot of the experiments in indie imsim design have been simply too janky for me to enjoy.

Part of the problem is I'm a highly tactile player, and my primary concern when playing any game is whether it feels good beneath the fingers. If a game falls at that initial hurdle, then it's likely (though not inevitable) that I'll drop it pretty quickly. Fortunately, I had the opposite experience with Deficit, an indie imsim with such a strong sense of physicality that I kept playing the demo despite some clear issues.

Developed by Item42, which previously created the cooperative shooter Perish, Deficit sees you play as a freelance spy in a dilapidated, dystopian world. You're tasked with infiltrating a sprawling fortress known as Hadrian's Wall to steal a device called the Interpolator, on behalf of a nameless client known as, well, The Client.

The premise is very Deus Ex, and Deficit involves a mix of sneaking and shooting similar to Ion Storm's cyberpunk classic. But Deficit's more specific inspiration is The Chronicles of Riddick: Escape from Butcher Bay, the surprisingly great tie-in game to David Twohy's mediocre Pitch Black sequel. Your character's melee attacks, which include wild swings of your fists and overhand jabs with makeshift knives—are hugely reminiscent of Riddick's brawling style in Starbreeze's cult 2004 hit.

While I'd need to go back to Butcher Bay to verify this, Deficit's brawling seems more physical than that of Butcher Bay. When you thwack a guard with a hammer, you can almost feel the impact shudder up your arm. Enemies are pleasingly reactive to being mercilessly beaten about the head too, stumbling and staggering before eventually collapsing in a pile of physics-powered limbs.

There's more to Deficit than just fisticuffs, though. You can throw objects to distract or damage guards, use batteries to activate and deactivate objects like doors and robotic sentries, lay traps using mines or laser tripwires, or shoot enemies with 3D-printed guns. The world is highly reactive too.

Nearby explosions won't just hurt you, but physically push you around, as I discovered when I got blasted backward through a doorway that I didn't know was behind me. Moreover, when I accidentally threw an object at a nearby wall, it bounced back, hit me in the face and dealt damage. Immersive sim confirmed.

Deficit definitely has potential. But there is one big problem—stealth. I can't tell whether the stealth system is broken or just incredibly hard to read, but I was constantly being spotted by enemies without really understanding why. They seemed to see me regardless of elevation and sometimes rumbled me despite there being an obstacle between us. As far as sneaking goes, Deficit needs a lot of work.

The good news is that Deficit is fun even with busted stealth, because playing aggressively is viable and satisfying to boot. There's no release date for Deficit at present, but you can play the demo right now, and I imagine we'll see the full version sometime next year.

articles.title: Is Apple working on its own game controller?
articles.subtitle: Macworld According to a sharp-eyed MacRumors reader, the first macOS 26.7 release candidate included references to a pair of game controllers. The same release candidate included code numbers for a slew of other in-development Apple products.
articles.author: Macworld Reviews
articles.content:
According to a sharp-eyed MacRumors reader, the first macOS 26.7 release candidate included references to a pair of game controllers. The same release candidate included code numbers for a slew of other in-development Apple products.

The two hardware devices are referenced as T6502 and T1057 and they include most standard game controller features: dual thumbsticks, face buttons, triggers, home and menu buttons, and different haptic features. One notable difference: the T1057 controller includes gryscope and accelerometer support (so games can tell how you tilt or move the controller) while T6502 does not.

While this is an interesting find, I caution readers not to assume that Apple is working on its own game controller. There have been rumors of Apple making its own game controller for over a decade, and nothing has ever come of it. Apple has instead done a lot to provide proper support for third-party game controllers, whether that’s its own MFi program or controllers for home console systems.

For years, you have been able to sync an Xbox or PlayStation controller to your Apple devices, including iPhones, iPads, Macs, and Apple TV. That includes the latest controllers for the Xbox Series X and PlayStation 5.

These code numbers probably reference test devices that are used in testing support for core game controller functions, or legacy references to R&D projects for Apple game controllers that may never be built. Apple famously has many products in various stages of development and only a few of them are ever released.

Apple could be building its own game controller, but there would be little reason to. Find My support and automatic switching between devices would be useful, but it’s hard to argue that modern controllers are missing features that require Apple to do its own thing. It makes much more sense for Apple to support the tens of millions of Xbox and PlayStation controllers than to make its own, especially as Apple’s platforms are not very popular for the kinds of games one usually plays with controllers.

articles.title: Perplexity Introduces ‘Hybrid Compute’ for Computer Agent on Apple Silicon Macs
articles.subtitle: Source: Perplexity. Perplexity has announced hybrid compute for Personal Computer on Apple silicon Macs. Personal Computer already combined cloud-based Computer tasks with access to local files and apps, but its AI processing was primarily cloud-based.
articles.author: MacStories
articles.content:
Perplexity has announced hybrid compute for Personal Computer on Apple silicon Macs. Personal Computer already combined cloud-based Computer tasks with access to local files and apps, but its AI processing was primarily cloud-based. Recently, Perplexity also introduced Portable Computer, a local-first version of Computer that can escalate work to the cloud with a user’s permission.

Hybrid compute approaches the problem from a different direction. Tasks start in the cloud but if a new local classifier detects potentially sensitive information, the user is alerted and asked whether they want to route it to a local model, although users also have the option to let the flagged data be used by a frontier cloud-based model. Gemma E4B, Qwen3.6 35B-A3B, and a Perplexity post-trained version of Qwen3.6 35B are available at launch for that local work, with more models to come in the future.

Tasks that don’t require sensitive information are handled in the cloud by frontier models that also orchestrate the cloud and local tasks. Users select the cloud orchestrator and Perplexity chooses the helper frontier models used.

Another key feature is that hybrid compute works with tasks begun from an iPhone or iPad, too. Those devices could already kick off a session, but now they can also run tasks that use sensitive information locally if your Mac is turned on and running Perplexity.

Yesterday, I got a demo of the feature that walked through three scenarios:

an attorney researching a legal brief, with sensitive client data on their Mac, allowing them to update it locally,

an analyst using web-based data to update a confidential slide deck for a presentation about a company’s financials, and

a small business owner kicking off pricing research from her iPhone that was combined with private pricing data for her business that never left her Mac.

I haven’t tried hybrid compute myself yet, but if it works as advertised, it’s a big step forward for Perplexity, and one that a lot of its competitors are also chasing. AI agents are only as good as the tools and data to which they have access.

Tool calling has been a big focus over the last year and more, but data privacy is an equally important issue that needs to be solved before more companies, especially those in regulated industries, adopt agentic tools like Personal Computer. It’s good to see Perplexity tackling this head-on.

articles.subtitle: Although the Siri app refuses to summarize webpages, the intelligent assistant can do so from within Safari. Similarly, it can summarise the content of YouTube videos from within the app – though the exact situation with both appears complex … The Siri...
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apple Intelligence
articles.content:
Although the Siri app refuses to summarize webpages, the intelligent assistant can do so from within Safari.

Similarly, it can summarise the content of YouTube videos from within the app – though the exact situation with both appears complex …

The Siri app refuses to summarize URLs

In the first developer beta, the Siri app would not summarise the content of a URL pasted into it. However, it would not explicitly refuse. This behavior changed in beta 2, with an explicit refusal.

A new section in Siri AI’s system prompt now says: “You cannot access content behind a URL. When a user provides a URL and asks you to summarize, read, or extract information from it, inform them that you cannot access web pages. Do not offer follow-up suggestions or workarounds.”

We speculated that this may be a deliberate decision on the company’s part in order to avoid robbing websites of visitors, which would make the web increasingly unsustainable over time.

Siri in Safari and YouTube will sometimes summarize

However, if you are inside the Safari app and ask Siri to “summarize this,” then it will do so at least some of the time. Other times, it will say it’s unable to do so.

It’s the same story inside the YouTube app, where Siri will sometimes summarise a video and other times say it is unable to do so.

9to5Mac’s Take

Given these differing behaviors, it’s not entirely clear what Apple intends the assistant to do in response to these requests. The fact that it’s a developer beta makes it harder still to differentiate intended behaviors from unexpected results, and we can expect further changes in future betas.

When we use the thumbs down feedback response, we can see a report which includes most of the sources used to answer the question. In the case of our own YouTube video, Siri has the 9to5Mac video channel as part of its world knowledge index, so it’s likely to be gathering the information from that. However, there are other occasions when it is very definitely examining the live webpage content – for example, reading a comment that has only just been posted.

We’ve reached out to Apple and will update with any response.

articles.title: When the Finder’s size ‘on disk’ is misleading
articles.subtitle: The Finder's Get Info figures allow for sparse files when giving size 'on disk', but don't take into account shared data in clone files. This can prove misleading, as shown here with VMs.
articles.author: The Eclectic Light Company
articles.content:
When I explained the meaning of the contents of the Finder’s Get Info dialog back in June, I noted: “Size “on disk” reflects the actual space allocated for that file’s data, which gets complicated with APFS special file types. For sparse files, it’s the actual space used, so should be significantly less than the nominal data size. However, that isn’t applied to clone files, where size “on disk” isn’t reduced to allow for storage blocks currently allocated to the data of more than one file.”

This article demonstrates an example where this becomes so misleading as to be nonsense.

Because of their space efficiency, I often duplicate virtual machine bundles. I keep a stock of those I use most commonly, including the current versions of Tahoe, Sequoia and Sonoma for testing apps in development. Before testing I duplicate the VM then use the cloned copy. VMs already use sparse files, and one with a nominal 100 GB disk capacity takes little more than 50 GB on disk. As the clone then only has to store what changes in that, it uses even less actual space.

For this test I started with a small container/partition just large enough to accommodate a VM in sparse file format and its clone. However, that has to be larger than the full non-sparse size of the VM, or the Finder refuses to copy it because there’s insufficient space. I therefore used a container of 120 GB to accommodate a VM of 107 GB taking only 53.83 GB on disk.

I then cloned that VM within the container. Ignoring the efficiencies of APFS, that should have brought the total size used in that 120 GB to 214.8 GB. In practice, Get Info reported:

the original VM was 107.41 GB, and used 53.83 GB on disk;

the clone was also 107.41 GB, and used 54.57 GB on disk.

Thus according to the Finder, total space used on disk should have been 108.4 GB out of 120 GB available, leaving just 11.6 GB free.

Disk Utility disagreed, because it’s able to take into account the space saved by the clone file. It reported 54.57 GB used, 65.3 GB available (with none purgeable), and 125.7 MB taken by ‘other volumes’. Thus, space actually used by the VMs was

for the original, 53.83 GB

for the clone, an additional 0.74 GB.

Although Disk Utility’s figures seemed reliable through much of this, it did have one strange episode shortly after cloning the VM, when it claimed that Other Volumes were taking -11.43 GB of space in that container.

I then set about increasing the space required by the cloned VM, first updating its macOS, then by filling it progressively with Stibium’s test files, until there was less than 1 GB available and macOS warned me of the problem.

Inside the VM, space available fell as low as 145.7 MB, with purgeable space of 22.3 MB, although none of that was ever purged, despite ample reason and opportunity. Instead, macOS just stopped writing files to disk. When I took a screenshot, for example, the image floated across the display then vanished instead of being saved to the Desktop.

Meanwhile the host reached 118. 88 GB used, with 993. 5 MB still available in that container. At that stage the clone VM’s use of disk space had risen from its original 0. 74 GB to 65. 05 GB. But the figures given by the Finder’s Get Info dialog were completely unchanged from its originals, and then underestimated the actual space taken on disk by the cloned VM by 10. 48 GB instead of overestimating them by 53.

83 GB. Maybe my suspicions would have been aroused had Get Info informed me that the VM was a clone, but as the Finder doesn’t seem able to do that either, I’d be left in the dark.

The problem arises because of the current implementation of clone files in APFS. Although file attributes do include a flag to indicate whether a file has ever been cloned, discovering which of a file’s extents are shared between two or more files as a result of cloning isn’t simple or quick enough to be taken into account when working out space taken on disk. Despite their great value, clone files will continue to result in misleading figures for file size.

In the Finder’s Get Info dialog, space given On Disk takes no account of that saved by clone files, but that given as Available in Disk Utility does, much of the time at least.

articles.content:
The deed is done! John Ternus is now CEO of Apple!

Memomento mori

[extreme TV infomercial announcer voice] Do you suffer from insomnia, sleeplessness, or the condition known as “Snooze Deficiency Syndrome”? “Read Tim Cook’s full memo to Apple employees on his last day as CEO”

Today is my last day as CEO of Apple.

Story checks out so far.

This is a moment I always knew would come one day…

BREAKING: FORMER APPLE CEO HAD FIRM GRASP OF THE LINEAR NATURE OF TIME.

…and yet it is still hard to believe it has arrived and I am writing these words.

[sound of 170,000 Apple employees closing an email and going back to whatever it was they were doing before]

If you’re not asleep yet, don’t worry. It goes on like that for kinda a while without saying much of anything. Again, though, if you’re not asleep by the end, don’t worry. Because Apple’s incoming CEO also has you covered.

“Read John Ternus’s full memo to Apple employees on his first day as CEO”

Hang on, I gotta get a cup of coffee before we read this because I’m already pretty groggy.

I’m honored to be stepping into this role at what is truly the greatest company in the world…

The greatest company in the world, the greatest network in the world, the greatest phone in the world…

Man, after reading these I feel like I really owe Stan Sigman an apology. Too late for that, I guess.

articles.title: Here's 10 more minutes of the most interesting game shown at this year's Opening Night Live
articles.subtitle: Rat's entertainment.
articles.author: PC Gamer
articles.content:
I was largely nonplussed by Gamescom's Opening Night Live, particularly its relentless barrage of identikit fantasy action games that I struggled to tell apart. But one game stood out like a rat-powered computer in an elven glade, and that was Ontos, Frictional Games' latest horror adventure/existential crisis generator.

The Gamescom trailer was a barrage of unsettling, distinctive imagery, from rodent server-racks to slack-jawed dudes with electrodes protruding from their heads. I was instantly intrigued and keen to learn more, so I was delighted to discover that Frictional graced us with a longer look at Ontos in action.

The 10-minute showcase focuses on the same part of the game as the shorter trailer. But it adds significant context to how Ontos plays and the kinds of challenges you'll be dealing with. It starts with the player character—a woman named Aditi—arriving at the hospital wing of Ontos' repurposed 'Moon Hotel' Samsara via an internal railway system, before exploring the wing and unpicking an experiment run by a scientist called Crombie.

In moment-to-moment play, Ontos shares a lot in common with most of Frictional's other games (the exception being Amnesia: The Bunker, which is more of a proto immersive sim). There's a lot of tactile environment interaction, poking around computers for text logs, and a grisly sequence where Aditi plucks some electrodes out of a live rat's exposed brain.

On top of this is a sprinkling of stealth, as Aditi evades a security camera by throwing a box across the room. Interestingly, the camera tracks the box's movement as it arcs through the air, which I'm sure must have featured in another game up to now. But I cannot recall an example of it.

Eventually, Aditi arrives at Crombie's experiment, which involves the rat server-rack seen in the Gamescom trailer. Crombie, speaking through the rat server, says he tried to create a copy of his personality to be stored in the rat RAM, but accidentally uploaded his consciousness from his own body, which sits slumped on a chair in the same room in a near-vegetative state.

He then asks Aditi to help him return his consciousness to his body. It's a reasonable request, provided the voice in the rat computer really does belong to the original Crombie.

Such philosophical dilemmas were exactly what made SOMA such a brilliant and unusual horror game, and the showcase has convinced me that Ontos' spin on these more intellectual scares will be worth a investigating the very least. The only thing I'm not totally sold on is Aditi's voice acting, which to me sounds a bit too chipper for someone confronted with such traumatic, reality-defying imagery.

In any case, 2027 can't come soon enough. Yet while Ontos was my favourite game shown at ONL, I wasn't quite the only thing that piqued my interest. Alien Isolation 2 seems to be shaping up to be a worthy successor to the original, as Joshua Wolens discovered in his hands-on demo. And naturally I'm up for one last adventure as Geralt of Rivia in The Witcher 3: Songs of the Past, which Joshua also saw in action in Cologne last month.

Ternus built his career quietly inside Apple

Corning CEO Wendell Weeks, who worked with Ternus during development of the original iPad, described him as talented, humble, and dedicated to excellence. Weeks also pointed to Ternus’s interest in racing cars as an example of the combination of passion and composure he brings to his work.

articles.title: Apple’s new Foundation Models explained: on-device AI, cloud AI, and everything in between
articles.subtitle: During the WWDC26 keynote, Apple announced its third generation of Apple Foundation Models (AFM), comprising five models, some of which are local, some of which are cloud-based, and one of which lives in Google’s servers running on Nvidia chips.
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apple Intelligence
articles.content:
During the WWDC26 keynote, Apple announced its third generation of Apple Foundation Models (AFM), comprising five models, some of which are local, some of which are cloud-based, and one of which lives in Google’s servers running on Nvidia chips. Here’s a breakdown of how that will work.

A bit of background

When Apple first announced its foundation models in 2024, the lineup included an on-device language model with roughly 3 billion parameters, and “a larger server-based language model available with Private Cloud Compute and running on Apple silicon servers,” as the company put it at the time.

Private Cloud Compute was an ambitious undertaking, as it aimed to deliver cloud-based AI capabilities while preserving the same privacy guarantees users expect from on-device processing.

For this reason, keeping everything in-house was essential. Private Cloud Compute ran in Apple data centers, on servers powered by Apple silicon. Even so, its privacy guarantees could be independently verified by third-party security researchers.

However, as Apple struggled to get its AI aspirations off the ground, the company partnered with Google to use Gemini as the backbone of its new AI efforts, the results of which it announced earlier this week during the WWDC26 keynote.

Apple’s new foundation models

The third generation of AFMs includes five models: AFM 3 Core and AFM 3 Code Advanced, which are on-device models, and AFM Cloud, ADM 3 Cloud (Image), and AFM 3 Cloud Pro, which are server-based. The D in ADM 3 Cloud (Image) stands for diffusion, a technology we’ve covered in the past here.

Except for AFM 3 Cloud Pro, all other models were built to run on Apple silicon devices. AFM 3 Cloud Pro, meanwhile, runs on NVIDIA GPUs hosted in Google Cloud.

This was made possible afer Apple extended its Private Cloud Compute architecture to third-party infrastructure for the first time, “while maintaining Apple’s powerful security and privacy protections,” according to the company.

As for the models themselves, here’s a breakdown of each one, as explained by Apple:

AFM 3 Core, the next generation of our 3-billion-parameter dense model that delivers a step up in quality. AFM 3 Core Advanced, our most powerful on-device model. It’s natively multimodal, enabling helpful features like expressive voices and higher-accuracy dictation.

Built on cutting-edge Apple research, this 20-billion-parameter model uses a sparse architecture, activating just 1 to 4 billion parameters at a time depending on the request. ADM 3 Cloud (Image), for image generation and editing, which unlocks advanced photo-editing tools, the all-new Image Playground, and more. AFM 3 Cloud Pro, our most capable server-based model, which powers our most demanding use cases, like agentic tool use and complex reasoning.

articles.title: Civilization 7 will finally enter the atomic age in 2027, via a free update Firaxis says will be 'even bigger in scope' than last year's Test of Time
articles.subtitle: First expansion "Earthrise" also announced.
articles.author: PC Gamer
articles.content:
Despite more than a year of updates and at least one massive overhaul, Civilization 7 remains as stubbornly divisive as ever. May's enormous Test of Time update brought significant mechanical reworks and a fresh influx of players to Firaxis' latest entry in the 4X series. But with Steam reviews still sitting at ' Mixed', with 51% positive, it ultimately did little to shift player opinion.

This is partly because numerous aspects of Civ 7 are still rudimentary compared to previous games, including the ability to wage nuclear war While Firaxis' latest allows players to drop atom bombs on their enemies via World War 2 bombers, its final, modern age ends in 1950, meaning many advanced technologies including nuclear submarines and ICBMs are not featured in the game.

Fortunately, this is going to change. Alongside the release of update 1.5.0 —which adds features like improved resource generation and an Earth map where your faction starts at their historically-accurate location—Firaxis outlined its plans for the sequel over the next 12 months. This includes another free update that will finally drag the game into the age of the A-bomb.

The update is called Arc of Tomorrow, and Firaxis says that it will be "even bigger in scope" than May's Test of Time patch. Introducing a fourth Act to Civ 7 that extends the game's timeline from 1950 to 2050, Arc of Tomorrow will bring a host of new features and play opportunities to the experience.

This includes "expanded nuclear gameplay" that introduces new units and what Firaxis describes as a "fun twist" on mutually assured destruction, plus atomic-era diplomacy options that will let players call for nuclear disarmament or escalate warhead production and send the doomsday clock spinning toward midnight.

Alongside nuclear weapons, the update will also extend Civ 7 into modernity in other ways. Firaxis says it will add the ability to transform settlements into City States, then use these to engage in proxy-wars to avoid battling empires directly, essentially letting you engage in Cold War-style conflicts.

It also introduces the ability to manufacture advanced resources like enriched uranium, and a system called "Great Works of Film", where film crews can scour the globe for ideal filming locations, presumably for cultural benefits.

Like Test of Time, Arc of Tomorrow will be free for all Civ 7 players. Unlike Test of Time, Arc of Tomorrow will likely be released alongside Civ 7's first major expansion—Earthrise. As the name suggests, this will focus on humanity's exploration of the stars.

Interestingly, your stellar endeavours will run throughout the game rather than being squashed into an end-game Space Age, with players able to chart the night sky in the age of antiquity and even name celestial bodies. As technology advances, you'll be able to launch your first orbital missions in the modern age, before establishing your own space agency in the modern age to venture out into the solar system.

Firaxis says that both the Earthrise expansion and the Arc of Tomorrow update will be released sometime in 2027, and that the announced features are still in development and subject to change.

In the meantime, if you're on the fence about Civilization 7 (and you certainly wouldn't be alone) the base game is currently free to play until September 10, so now would be a good time to see whether its structure works for you. If you're taken with it, then the full game is 50% off until September 17, down from $70 (£60) to $35 (£30).

articles.title: Apple Arcade in September: Four new games added to the service again this month
articles.subtitle: Macworld Gaming subscription services are all the rage now, but Apple Arcade isn’t a little different from the likes of PlayStation Plus, EA Play, or Xbox Game Pass. If you’ve got questions about it, we’ve got plenty of answers.
articles.author: Macworld Reviews
articles.content:
Gaming subscription services are all the rage now, but Apple Arcade isn’t a little different from the likes of PlayStation Plus, EA Play, or Xbox Game Pass. If you’ve got questions about it, we’ve got plenty of answers.

Updated September 4, 2026: There are four new games on the service again this month: Art of Fauna: Cozy Puzzles+, Block Blast+, Coloring Games for Families+, and Let’s Play! Oink Games+.

What is Apple Arcade?

Apple Arcade is a gaming subscription service for iPhone, iPad, Mac, and AppleTV that features several hundred games. The games are a mix of genres and styles, and include original games you’ll only find on the service and others that can be found on the regular App Store or even other platforms. Apple Arcade isn’t a streaming service like Xbox Live Cloud Gaming or GeForce NOW. Games must be downloaded onto your device in order to be played.

What do I need to run it?

Apple Arcade was made available as part of iOS 13, iPad OS 13, tvOS 13, and macOS Catalina or later. Some of the more visually-intensive games may only run well on newer hardware, though, and some Mac games require macOS 11 (Big Sur).

How much does Apple Arcade cost?

Apple Arcade costs $6.99/£6.99 per month, and you’ll also get a one-month free trial or you can get three months free if you purchase a new iPhone, iPad, Apple TV or Mac. To claim your free trial click here.

You can get Apple Arcade for less than $6.99 a month if you subscribe for a year upfront. A year of Apple Arcade is $49.99/£49.99 (so $4.16 a month). If you’re currently on the $6.99 month-to-month plan and want to switch to the annual plan and save some money, you can do so on your iPhone or iPad. Open the App Store app, then tap your account icon in the upper right. Tap Subscriptions, then tap the entry for Apple Arcade. Here, you can switch to the annual plan.

Apple Arcade is also included in the Apple One subscription bundles, which range from $20 a month to $38 a month and include access to Apple Music and Apple TV and iCloud storage. There is also a month free trial of Apple One. To claim the trial, or sign up for Apple One, click here.

How do I sign up for Apple Arcade?

There isn’t an Apple Arcade app—it’s built into the App Store. On your iPhone, iPad, or Mac open the App Store and look for the Apple Arcade tab at the bottom of the screen (or in the left column on macOS). A sign-up screen with a Try It Free button will appear. After the trial you’ll be charged either the monthly or annual fee, depending on your selection.

When subscribing, you’ll need to enter your Apple ID password or use Touch ID or Face ID to sign in, and you’ll have to confirm your subscription purchase a few times.

Once you’re done with the sign up, the Arcade section of the App Store shows what games are available to you. To access a game, tap on it in the App Store, then tap the Get button. When the game is done installing on your device, the Get button turns into a Play button, and you can tap it to launch the game. The game app icon will also appear on your device’s Home page.

On the Apple TV, there actually is an Arcade app. Open that to see the sign-up offer. You’ll also find an Arcade tab within the App Store.

Does my subscription include family sharing?

Yes. One $6.99 per month subscription can be shared between up to six people (including you).

articles.title: The Potential of M6 and M5 Ultra for Local AI on macOS
articles.subtitle: Earlier today, Apple unveiled the new generation of Mac mini and Mac Studio, featuring the latest entries in the Apple silicon family of chips: the M6, available in the Mac mini, and the M5 Ultra, exclusive to the Mac Studio.
articles.author: MacStories
articles.content:
Earlier today, Apple unveiled the new generation of Mac mini and Mac Studio, featuring the latest entries in the Apple silicon family of chips: the M6, available in the Mac mini, and the M5 Ultra, exclusive to the Mac Studio. You can read more details about the announcement and related specs in John’s overview.

As someone who’s been working with an M3 Ultra Mac Studio (on loan from Apple) with 512 GB of RAM for the past year (plus two separate M4 Mac minis) with a particular focus on local AI models and performance gains enabled by Apple’s MLX framework, I obviously am very interested in these new machines.

To give you some context: my current workspace for my upcoming iOS and iPadOS 27 review, which lives in Notion, is entirely managed by a series of local agents running the latest DeepSeek-V4-Flash via MLX on the Mac Studio, which continuously scan the project for new notes, sources, and research material that is automatically categorized and linked in the chapters that I’m writing.

So, yes, I’m sure I’ll have more thoughts on the new Mac minis and Mac Studios soon. In the meantime, I thought it’d be fun to break down the local AI-related details from Apple.

First, the M6. While it may not be the powerhouse that the M5 Ultra is, it’s an interesting new chip because of its new 2 nm process and dual Neural Engine system:

M6 is built using cutting-edge 2 nm process technology, packing greater transistor density into a smaller die for a major leap in performance and power efficiency. M6 also introduces a Dual 16-core Neural Engine, providing up to 2x the peak compute over previous generations to make on-device AI workflows run even faster. System frameworks can automatically utilize both engines simultaneously, enabling applications to see faster model execution.

But that’s not all: the new 12-core GPU (which has two more cores than the M4’s old GPU) now features Neural Accelerators in each core for the first time on the Mac mini. The result, according to Apple, is “4x faster AI performance and 2x faster graphics than Mac mini with M4”. If these numbers hold up and scale linearly, a local Mixture-of-Experts model such as Qwen 3.

5-35B-A3B, which would run at ~17 tokens/sec on average on a base M4 Mac mini with 16 GB of RAM, could realistically generate output at over 60 tokens/second with the base model M6 Mac mini.

Based on what we’ve seen so far, the one downside of the M6 Mac mini is that it does not have Thunderbolt 5 ports; those are exclusive to the M5 Pro model, also announced today. As Apple also notes, Thunderbolt 5 allows multiple M5 Pro Mac minis to run local AI models as a single cluster (for example, using something like exo ).

Alas, that won’t be possible with the M6 Mac mini and its Thunderbolt 4 bandwidth bottleneck. Nonetheless, I’d be intrigued to compare the performance of the widely regarded Qwen3. 8-27B and DeepSeek-V4-Flash models on the new M6 Mac mini.

Moving on to the flagship M5 Ultra Mac Studio, let’s start here:

With M5 Ultra, Mac Studio achieves up to 4.3x the peak AI compute performance of M3 Ultra and a staggering 9.8x more than M1 Ultra. Combined with up to 512GB of unified memory and 1.2TB/s of memory bandwidth, 50 percent higher than before, Mac Studio lets users run massive models entirely on device with complete privacy — without counting tokens or worrying about rising cloud costs.

As seen on the Mac Studio’s product page, the 512 GB RAM version of the M5 Ultra Mac Studio will only be available in “late October”. Unlike the M6, the M5 Ultra supports Thunderbolt 5, which will allow customers to run multiple Mac Studios in a cluster with shared memory to distribute inference across machines. And, according to Apple, a cluster of four Mac Studios yields three times the performance of a single Mac Studio.

Speaking from personal experience, I know that my M3 Ultra Mac Studio using oMLX can run DeepSeek-V4-Flash locally with generation averaging 35 tokens/second. Assuming a linear 4x increase, that would put the same model at over 120 tokens/second on an M5 Ultra Mac Studio.

To put things in perspective, that kind of performance would be faster than any AI chatbot website, it’d be faster than many providers who offer a “fast” mode for their models, and it’d only be second to either dedicated NVIDIA PC clusters at home or specialized inference providers such as Cerebras or Groq …which are running in full-blown data centers.

Sure, you would need a computer that is likely going to cost more than $20,000 to make it happen, but it’d still be possible on a single machine that is small, quiet, and that – in theory – any consumer can buy off the shelf.

It’s also interesting to consider the implications of M5 Ultra for running much larger models that would have typically required aggressive quantization to even stay in memory and produce any useful output. For example, Z. ai’s GLM-5.

2 (a 744B MoE model) could run at up to 17 tokens/second on an M3 Ultra Mac Studio with 512 GB of RAM; the same person was even able to get the massive Kimi K3 model to run on a single machine…with decoding performance up to 3 tokens/second.

articles.title: 3 Games Where Your Choices Truly Matter
articles.subtitle: And no, I don't mean Baldur's Gate and Mass Effect The way Rebel Wolves promoted The Blood of Dawnwalker and its myriad choices got me thinking: What does it really mean for your choices to matter in a video game?
articles.author: Polygon
articles.content:
And no, I don't mean Baldur's Gate and Mass Effect

The way Rebel Wolves promoted The Blood of Dawnwalker and its myriad choices got me thinking: What does it really mean for your choices to matter in a video game? Typically, we think it's a good use of branching narratives when you have a properly big, dramatic effect on how things play out or when you have hundreds of endings.

Just look at how so much attention on Baldur's Gate 3 focused on the endings or, further back in time, how everyone tends to ignore the smaller ways the Mass Effect trilogy changed in favor of looking at the restrictive outcomes in Mass Effect 3.

Large-scale narrative branches are engaging for a reason. They're satisfying, and they make you feel a sense of influence over events and characters you care about. Like with video game romance, however, they have become somewhat stale and predictable in form. So for this list, I decided to look at three games that use branching narratives in bolder and unexpected ways.

3 Zero Parades: For Dead Spies

Zero Parades: For Dead Spies is the rare piece of interactive media where your choices matter not just for how they influence the story, but for how they shape your actions, too. Hershel, the protagonist of the piece, is a spy. Or, was a spy. A series of catastrophic incidents happened, and she finds herself decommissioned, in a room with a comatose person, and without any idea how she got here.

There's a very dangerous game afoot in the fictional town of Portofiro, Zero Parades ' setting, and your job is figuring it out and possibly even finding redemption. Maybe. If you can manage it.

Like its spiritual predecessor Disco Elysium, Zero Parades has standard CRPG elements like persuasion and knowledge, but unlike standard CRPGs, you're doing a lot more with them other than picking locks and lying to folks. With higher points in certain social or mental skills, you have a better chance of passing certain checks in conversations that unlock entirely new perspectives on what's happening.

Sometimes, you just get a bit of extra lore. That's usually like the consolation prize in video games, but Zero Parades ' impeccable writing means these moments are just as rewarding as stumbling onto a new story path.

On other occasions, you fall down a rabbit hole of madness and form a bond with a drunken businessman over your shared delusions about the idea of a goddess trampling you underfoot (for example). Which sounds fun, and it is, until your delusion stat maxes out and you die. The same can happen with fatigue and anxiety stats. Just like real life!

Balancing your more extreme decisions with less tumultuous ones is a big part of Zero Parades, but whatever choice you make, it always takes a "yes, and" approach. Even when what you've done seems very wrong, possibly even fatal, you nearly always have a way forward. It might just be very, very different from the path you thought you'd take.

It keeps you in a state of perpetual uncertainty, like you have no idea what the right thing to do is and just have to wing it and hope for the best. In other words, you're thinking and behaving just like Hershel. I can't think of any other game that uses choices to let you embody a character on such an important level — not even the (also excellent) Disco Elysium.

2 Slay the Princess

The duo at Black Tabby love pushing the boundaries of choice-driven narratives, so in the middle of making the massive Scarlet Hollow, they set out to do something more contained and experimental with Slay the Princess. You're a valiant warrior, tasked with entering a cabin, descending to its basement, and slaying the princess imprisoned there. She is, the narrator assures you, quite dangerous.

Not human at all, but a fiendish monster adopting the guise of an innocent maiden. What you do from here ripples out across the rest of the game in wildly unforeseen ways. Even refusing to enter the cabin is a valid choice, one that unlocks a whole new branch of the story.

When folks talk about games where choices matter, the conversation typically heads in one direction: how many endings there are. It's the logical endpoint of wondering how your choices will or won't matter. However, it overlooks other, equally important ways stories change based on how you interact with them. Slay the Princess embodies the best of both philosophies.

The many and varied branches eventually resolve into a fixed set of potential endings, but the outcome is only half the story, or not even half, really. Each path — even the ones that share the same outcome — unfolds around some new facet of the situation, or yourself, or the princess, or a combination of all those things.

You make your choices guided solely by your instincts and what you're encouraged to believe based on other interactions. (E.g., if the princess murders you brutally in one run, you're a lot less likely to believe her protestations of innocence the next time.) It gives these branches an intensity that's unique to Slay the Princess and utterly impossible to have in a story where you're just wondering who lives or dies based on what you do.

articles.title: Touchscreen MacBook Pro rumours: Release date, OLED, specs and latest leaks
articles.subtitle: Macworld The touchscreen MacBook Pro has been the subject of speculation ever since Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman first reported in 2023 that Apple was exploring the idea.
articles.author: Macworld Reviews
articles.content:
The touchscreen MacBook Pro has been the subject of speculation ever since Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman first reported in 2023 that Apple was exploring the idea. At the time, the claim seemed hard to believe given Apple’s long-standing opposition to touchscreen laptops. Three years later, however, the rumours are becoming increasingly difficult to dismiss.

Multiple reports suggest Apple has overcome the technical and design challenges that previously stood in the way. If they’re accurate, the first touchscreen MacBook Pro will arrive as part of one of the biggest redesigns in the laptop’s history, combining a new chassis with Apple’s first OLED MacBook display, next-generation Apple silicon, and potentially even an iPhone-style Dynamic Island camera cutout.

The timing would be fitting. The MacBook Pro celebrates its 20th anniversary in 2026, and Apple could mark the milestone with a feature many believed would never come to the Mac. Touchscreen support would also help further differentiate the MacBook Pro from the MacBook Air and the rumoured budget-friendly MacBook Neo.

There are still questions over pricing. OLED panels and ongoing supply-chain pressures are expected to make the new models more expensive than today’s MacBook Pro. Apple is also expected to keep touchscreen technology exclusive to its premium laptops initially, with no indication that it will come to the MacBook Air or MacBook Neo in the first generation.

Read on for a complete roundup of the latest touchscreen MacBook Pro rumours, including what the most reliable sources are saying, how credible each report is, and what we think Apple is likely to announce and when.

Touchscreen MacBook Pro release date: When will it launch?

Late 2026 planned

Early 2027 a possibility

While Apple has yet to officially confirm the device, reports from respected analysts, supply-chain sources, and references discovered in Apple’s software all suggest development is well underway. The company is widely expected to launch a redesigned MacBook Pro featuring its first touchscreen OLED display in either late 2026 or early 2027.

In September 2026, Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman included the touchscreen MacBooks in a list of products that will ship in late 2026/early 2027.

Earlier rumours pointed firmly to a launch in the second half of 2026. Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman and analyst Ming-Chi Kuo both initially predicted a late 2026 debut, with an October announcement fitting Apple’s traditional MacBook Pro release schedule while also coinciding with the 20th anniversary of the MacBook Pro’s introduction.

In January, South Korean blog Naver reported that Samsung had begun production on its new 8. 6-generation OLED manufacturing line, which is expected to supply panels for the next-generation MacBook Pro, further supporting that timeframe. Gurman also reported in February that the redesigned MacBook Pro would arrive in the “back half” of 2026.

However, a launch in early 2027 now appears more likely. Global DRAM and NAND shortages, which prompted Apple to raise Mac and iPad prices in June 2026 – are expected to continue well into 2027. In April, Gurman reported that supply-chain constraints were affecting development of the redesigned MacBook Pro and could push the release into until early 2027.

He subsequently reported in June that Apple had revised its chip roadmap, with the touchscreen MacBook Pro now expected to launch with M5 Pro and M5 Max chips instead of M6 Pro and M6 Max in an effort to keep the project on schedule.

In a July report, Gurman reiterated that these laptops are planned for this fall, but a 2027 ship date is possible.

Taken together, the continuing component shortages, Apple’s revised silicon plans, and the scale of the redesign make early 2027 the more likely launch window, although a late 2026 release has not yet been ruled out.

Which MacBook models will get a touchscreen?

Current rumours suggest that Apple’s first touchscreen laptop will be a redesigned MacBook Pro with Pro and Max chips

articles.title: Apple Announces New M6 and M5 Pro Mac minis, Along with M5 Max and M5 Ultra Mac Studios
articles.subtitle: Source: Apple. Today, Apple announced a new M6 chip that will debut in the Mac mini and an M5 Ultra that is coming to the Mac Studio. The company also announced an M5 Pro Mac mini and an M5 Max Mac Studio. Let’s take a look at the headline specs.
articles.author: MacStories
articles.content:
Today, Apple announced a new M6 chip that will debut in the Mac mini and an M5 Ultra that is coming to the Mac Studio. The company also announced an M5 Pro Mac mini and an M5 Max Mac Studio. Let’s take a look at the headline specs.

The headline feature of the M6 chip is that it’s Apple’s first 2-nanometer chip. The chip also includes “a larger 12-core CPU complex with the world’s fastest CPU core, a larger 12-core GPU with Neural Accelerators, a Dual 16-core Neural Engine, and up to 170GB/s of unified memory bandwidth.”

Looking more closely at the M6, Apple says it consists of two super cores, four performance cores, and six efficiency cores and is 1.2x faster in multithreaded performance than an M5 and up to 2.4x faster than an M1. Apple says the GPU delivers nearly 30% more peak GPU compute for AI than the M5. The M6’s 10% faster memory bandwidth will help with AI tasks, too, but its 32GB memory ceiling will limit which models can run locally.

The M6 mini’s GPU sounds impressive, too, with two more cores, Neural Accelerators for each core, which is a first for the mini. According to Apple, that leads to an up to four-fold increase in AI performance and a 2x graphics bump compared to the M4 mini. The Neural Engine has also been improved.

Apple also introduced an M5 Pro mini. It’s understandable if you find it confusing that the base model Mac mini has a more recent generation chipset than the more expensive model. What matters more than the chip generation is the “Pro” in M5 Pro, which makes it more capable than the M6, which has been designed for entry-level models.

The same sort of asymmetry occurred with the 2025 Mac Studio, which included an M4 Max model alongside the M3 Ultra. A big part of that difference is the M5 Pro mini’s support for 64GB of memory (double the M6 version’s top memory spec) and its 307GB/s of memory bandwidth compared to the M6 model’s 170GB/s memory bandwidth.

As for the M5 Ultra, which debuts in the Mac Studio, it sounds like a beast. According to Apple, the chip uses a next-generation version of its UltraFusion technology, resulting in a quad-die architecture for the first time in an Apple silicon chip. In addition, the M5 Ultra features an “up-to-36-core CPU and up-to-80-core GPU with a massive 1.2TB/s of unified memory bandwidth, 50 percent more than M3 Ultra.”

Here’s what Sri Santhanam, Apple’s vice president of Silicon Engineering Group, had to say about the new chips:

Today, we’re debuting the next giant leap in performance and AI compute for Apple silicon with the incredibly advanced M6 and the most powerful M-series chip yet, M5 Ultra. Built using the cutting-edge 2 nm process, M6 combines a new CPU complex, two additional CPU and GPU cores, a Dual 16-core Neural Engine, and more unified memory bandwidth to power through workloads with amazing energy efficiency.

And for the ultimate desktop performance and the ability to run massive AI models, M5 Ultra features a massive GPU, now with Neural Accelerators, and more unified memory bandwidth, pushing the boundaries of what a desktop can do.

Apple is fusing two dual-die M5 Max chips to create a single quad-die architecture. Apple says the M5 Ultra is “up to 1.25x higher single-threaded performance and up to 1.3x higher multithreaded performance than M3 Ultra”, the fastest Mac previously for sale. The M5 Ultra also supports up to an 80-core GPU with up to 4.5x the peak GPU compute for AI tasks compared to the M3 Ultra and features an upgraded Media Engine, according to Apple.

For those who don’t need the bleeding-edge performance of the M5 Ultra, Apple also introduced what sounds like a very capable M5 Max Mac Studio. The M5 Max version of the computer “features an 18-core CPU, an up-to-40-core GPU with Neural Accelerators built into each core, and up to 128GB of unified memory, accelerating complex pro and AI workloads.”

Macs featuring the new chips won’t be available immediately. You can preorder both online today for delivery on September 22 with the caveat that the M5 Ultra Mac Studio with 512GB of memory won’t be available until later in October.

Prices have risen too. The Mac mini models are both $100 more than the models they replace, while the M5 Ultra Mac Studio’s base configuration has risen $200. However, the M5 Max Mac Studio’s starting price hasn’t changed.

The Mac mini has been a lot of things to a lot of people over the years. From a compact, minimalist desktop system to a headless server, the mini is Apple’s jack-of-all-trades. More recently, demand for the tiny computer has surged as people put them to work for a variety of AI tasks, including running LLMs locally and serving as standalone Hermes and OpenClaw machines.

With memory and storage constraints, it’s no surprise that the base prices of the mini have risen. Despite those challenges, I hope Apple is able to produce enough to meet demand. I’ve loved having an M4 Pro model working away day and night in the background. It’s fast, relatively cool, energy efficient, and easy to run remotely.

If the claims of Apple’s press release hold up under real-world use, I expect the new models will be the same, but faster and more capable, which is especially important for tasks like running models locally.

I’m also looking forward to seeing how the new Mac Studios perform in real world tests. I’ve used an M1 Max Mac Studio for a few years now and it’s been every bit the workhorse computer I need for my day-to-day work. However, it’s beginning to show its age when it comes to AI tasks, coding, and other tasks. It may finally be time for me to upgrade.
